source.title: Memorizing without overfitting: Bias, variance, and interpolation in overparameterized models

record.tranche_reason: The study analytically derives and simulates test-error behavior across model sizes in two simplified model families. This tests double descent with a different method and model setting from the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own analytic and simulation results for model-size sweeps and bias-variance behavior. Results it cites about deep networks, sample-wise double descent, or triple descent are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study derives exact asymptotic training and test error, bias and variance, with matching simulations, across a parameters-to-data sweep in ridgeless linear regression and a random nonlinear-features model. This is a different method aimed at whether risk peaks at interpolation and falls again, and at what drives the peak. The random-features model has a fixed random hidden layer and a trained top layer, so it is a kernel-like model, not a trained deep network.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that in both minimal models, variance peaks (diverges) at the interpolation threshold and then decreases, producing double descent, tied to small Hessian eigenvalues. Bias stays finite: in the random-features model it decreases monotonically, so both bias and variance fall past the threshold. In linear regression, bias instead rises beyond the threshold (an 'inverted' trade-off). Bias can arise from incomplete feature sampling even when teacher and student match. Biased models can overfit without label noise. Interpolation is shown to be separable from overfitting. They note the limits of the lazy regime and convex losses.
record.recipe_differences: Uses zero-temperature cavity analysis and numerical simulations of ridgeless linear regression and a two-layer random nonlinear-features model, rather than empirical size sweeps of practical deep networks.
record.method_sensitivity: For the random nonlinear-features model, whether canonical double descent appears depends on αf: the paper reports it for αf < 1 but not αf > 1. It also reports different bias behavior for linear regression and the random nonlinear-features model.

fits_no_version.finding: The interpolation threshold coincides with the minimum nonzero Hessian eigenvalue going to zero. Over-parameterization reopens a spectral gap, and this tracks the variance peak in both models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The double-descent peak coincides with the smallest nonzero eigenvalue of the feature covariance approaching zero at interpolation.

fits_no_version.finding: Under standard bias-variance definitions, bias in the random-features model decreases monotonically through and beyond the threshold. Fixed-design or ensemble definitions instead give a diverging bias or a bias that plateaus at the threshold (Sec. V F, Fig. S2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Past interpolation, both bias and variance decrease in random-features models when standard decompositions are used.

record.problems: The models are simplified and operate in the lazy regime with a convex loss; the paper notes that this differs from practical deep learning in feature learning and non-convexity. Some results are supported by plots and qualitative descriptions rather than tabulated values.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying own-result rows were left out. Cited results from other work, including sample-wise double descent and triple descent, were excluded.

untested.parts: No trained deep network is studied. The random-features model fixes its hidden layer and is kernel-like (lazy regime, convex loss).
Test error over training epochs is not studied; models are solved in closed form.
Sample count is not varied as an intervention; results are expressed only through ratios αf and αp.
Only ridgeless linear regression and random features with ReLU are tested. Other model classes are not, and neither are non-convex or feature-learning settings.
No effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting the peak across axes. The threshold is located at Np = M by construction.
Regularization strength is not varied (λ → 0 or 10^-6 only), so removal of the peak under optimal regularization is untested. Triple or multiple descent is not tested; the paper only cites it.
The curve is not re-expressed against an effective parameter count.

missing.what: Test error for the random-features model as a function of both αp and αf, showing divergence along the whole αp = 1 boundary, including αf > 1. This is needed to correct R2's state.
missing.locator: Sec. IV C; Fig. 3(d); Fig. S1(b)

missing.what: Over-parameterized test-error behavior in linear regression: non-monotonic, rising toward σβ²σX² as αf grows (Eq. 28). The R3 value omits this.
Explicit statement that without label noise, test error diverges at interpolation only if the model is biased.
missing.locator: Sec. V C, paragraph after Fig. 5 discussion

record.verdict_notes: V1 was dropped from all rows: random features with a fixed random hidden layer are kernel-like, not trained deep networks, so they bear on V4 rather than V1. Some researchers may read the two-layer framing more loosely. Neither original source is this paper. All results are analytic in the thermodynamic limit, with simulations at M = 512 and λ = 10^-6. Regularization is never tuned, so V6's regularization clause is untested.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests model-size behavior in a two-layer random nonlinear-features model with a fixed random hidden layer, not practical deep networks generally. It does not test other size axes or training epochs.
Test error over training epochs is not measured.
The study does not vary training sample size as an independent intervention to test whether more data raises test error near interpolation.
Tests linear regression and a random nonlinear-features model only; it does not establish behavior across model classes generally.
The study does not test whether one measure of effective complexity predicts the peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.

The study analyzes variance and label-noise contributions and presents a biased, noise-free case. It does not test triple or multiple descent, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
The study does not re-express the curve using an effective parameter count to test whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shape.

rows.size_stated: Np fit parameters/hidden features; M = 512 in simulations
rows.operation_detail: Sweep fit-parameter-to-data ratio αp = Np/M and measure test error

conditions.value: λ = 10^-6 in simulations; analytic results in the ridgeless limit

rows.value: The test error diverges at αp = 1 and shows canonical double descent when αf < 1.
rows.uncertainty: Simulation error bars indicate error on the mean; plots average 1000 simulations except 150000 at a phase transition.

rows.note: The model has random, fixed middle-layer weights and a trained top layer. The paper identifies αp = 1 as the interpolation threshold.
rows.check: Linked to V1, but the subject is a random-features model with fixed random middle weights and only the top layer fitted (a linear model with basis functions), not a trained deep network. It bears on V4 (other model classes), not V1.

rows.subject: Random nonlinear features model (two-layer nonlinear neural network)
rows.size_stated: Np fit parameters/hidden features; M is the training-set size
rows.operation_detail: Sweep αp = Np/M at feature-to-data ratios αf > 1
rows.measure: Test error as a function of model size
rows.value: The paper says canonical double descent occurs only when αf < 1; for αf > 1 the test error shows only a small qualitative difference between regimes.
rows.note: The reported result does not describe a canonical fall-rise-fall test-error curve for this condition.
rows.check: State 'absent' overstates. The text says test error diverges at every point along the αp = 1 boundary, including αf > 1, and variance accounts for this. Only the canonical fall-rise-fall shape is missing. The peak and the post-threshold decrease persist, so this is partial. Not V1, for the same reason as R1.

rows.subject: Linear regression (no basis functions)
rows.operation_detail: Sweep feature and parameter ratio αf = Nf/M = Np/M

conditions.value: λ = 10^-6 in simulations; analytic results in the ridgeless limit

rows.value: Test error diverges at αf = 1 and then decreases in the over-parameterized regime.
rows.uncertainty: Simulation error bars indicate error on the mean; plots average 1000 simulations except 150000 at a phase transition.
rows.note: Here model size and feature count are tied: Np = Nf.
rows.check: The value omits what Eq. (28) shows for the linear teacher. Below the threshold, test error rises monotonically (no first descent). Beyond it, error falls and then rises toward σβ²σX², which exceeds the under-parameterized minimum at SNR 10. The paper calls this decrease 'non-monotonic'. The peak and second descent exist, but only partially in the V4 sense.

rows.subject: Linear regression (no basis functions)
rows.operation_detail: Compare bias and variance contributions across model size with a nonlinear teacher
rows.measure: Squared bias and prediction variance, decomposed by label component
rows.value: The linear-label and nonlinear-label contributions to bias each have a corresponding variance contribution across αf; label noise also contributes to variance.
rows.uncertainty: Simulation error bars indicate error on the mean.
rows.note: The paper interprets bias-related signal as a source of variance, in addition to variance from label noise.
rows.check: The value is vague. The key reported fact is that each bias source has a matching variance term for every αf. In the absence of noise, variance is zero only when bias is zero.

rows.subject: Linear regression (no basis functions)
rows.size_stated: Np = Nf = M at the interpolation threshold
rows.operation_detail: Compare the fitted relationship along the minimum principal component with and without label noise
rows.measure: Overfitting in the learned relationship along the minimum principal component
rows.baseline: The expected relationship for an average test set
rows.value: The model still overfits in the absence of label noise when the teacher and student models do not match.
rows.note: The authors attribute this noise-free overfitting to model bias.
rows.check: This is a qualitative scatter-plot demonstration (Fig. 5f), not a test-error rate. The text generalizes it: without label noise, test error diverges at interpolation only if the model is biased.

tranche.reason: Cavity analysis and numerical simulations directly test interpolation peaks and subsequent risk reduction using minimal regression models.

source_check.notes: R9–R10 are qualitative principal-component demonstrations; absent overfitting in R10 is a consistent control, not evidence against V6. Their scatter plots use M = M′ = 200, while the error and variance sweeps use 512.

statements.correction: Noiseless tanh-teacher linear regression: overfitting at interpolation; noiseless linear-teacher control: no overfitting. Misspecified signal contributes prediction variance. These results support V6's variance mechanism while refuting label-noise necessity.
statements.problem: The study-specific facts are correct, but classifying them as limits_scope against V6 is unsupported: V6 permits variance-driven peaks without label noise.
